title_en: French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living
title_zh: 法国抗议人数激增，工会因生活成本高而参加罢工
summary: The interior ministry estimates 600,000 people joined protests across France, while the unions say the number was far higher.
summary_zh: 内政部估计法国各地有 60 万人参加了抗议活动，而工会则表示这个数字要高得多。
body_en: More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.

The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.
As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.

The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.

The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.

Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.

The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.
Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise Léon, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.

A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently €12.31 (£10) an hour.
Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of €100 a month," Marylise Léon explained.

The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".
However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.
body_zh: 据法国内政部称，法国各地已有超过 60 万抗议者参加集会和游行，其中五个工会参加了一天的行动，要求增加工资和公共服务资金。
左翼总工会估计参加周四动员的人数为157万人，并称赞这一数字是自2023年以来“无与伦比的水平”，并列举了巴黎、马赛、波尔多和里尔的大规模抗议活动。
当巴黎夜幕降临时，总理塞巴斯蒂安·勒科尔努表示，他将于下周一与工会和雇主召开“社交会议”。
抗议浪潮始于 9 月份，原因是高中条件恶劣，资源匮乏，随后蔓延至大学、工人以及反对高物价的“黄背心”运动死灰复燃。
工会发誓要将反对政府的协调行动“提升到一个新的水平”，总工会主席索菲·比内表示，他们的信息是“唯一能让这场动员停止的就是回应我们的要求”。
内政部长洛朗·努涅斯早些时候部署了 70,000 名警察，誓言对任何潜在的暴力事件“采取极其坚决的反应”。
里昂罗纳河上的加列尼桥附近，一辆汽车被点燃，数百名来自激进左翼“黑人集团”的活动人士与警方发生冲突。
据报道，西北部城市雷恩也发生了冲突，当地省长表示，一群“敌对的蒙面人”聚集在工会主要游行队伍前。西南城市波尔多的一个广场被使用催泪瓦斯清理，巴黎北部塞纳-圣但尼郊区的一所高中封锁区发生了一起涉及一名学生的刺伤事件，一名青少年受伤。
但问题的规模并未达到抗议活动最后一个重要日子（10 月 17 日星期六）的规模，当时 2000 多家商店被抢劫，历史建筑被纵火。
周四报告的临时数字高于 10 月 17 日，10 月 17 日被认为是迄今为止集会人数最多的一天，当时内政部称参加集会的人数为 55 万人，工会统计的人数为 80 万人。
周四早些时候，CFDT 工会领导人 Marylise Léon 表示，如果抗议活动达到之前的水平，她会很高兴。
公共和私营部门的工会联盟敦促工人、养老金领取者和年轻人参加周四的罢工，以加大对政府的压力。他们特别寻求提高最低工资（Smic），目前为每小时 12.31 欧元（10 英镑）。
索菲·比奈在巴黎市中心的游行开始时告诉记者，抗议者“动员程度刚刚达到一个新水平”，并要求立即得到答复。
根据政府数据，估计有 9.89% 的公务员参加了罢工。
据报道，学校、医院和公共交通受到干扰，埃菲尔铁塔和巴黎卢浮宫的一些展览室不得不关闭。
炼油厂的工人也被要求停止生产，由于核电站中断，预计法国进口的电力将超过周四的产量。
CFDT 负责人抱怨说，需要提高的不仅仅是最低工资。 “我们要求每月净增加 100 欧元，”Marylise Léon 解释道。
政府试图平息公众对价格上涨的愤怒，从战略储备中释放了1000万桶柴油来降低燃料成本。部长们还向学生承诺改革不受欢迎的 Parcoursup 大学招生平台，并最终在 2028 年之前取代它。
总理周四晚间早些时候表示，周一与工会和雇主举行的“社交会议”将寻求“提供有关购买力和工资问题的答案”。
然而，政府自己也承认，回旋余地很小，因为它希望节省数百亿欧元，以将预算赤字削减至GDP的5%。

title_en: Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
title_zh: Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
summary: Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.
summary_zh: Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.
body_en: Share Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday on social media

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.
He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.
Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.
Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, ⁠but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.
Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.
Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.

“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.

Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.
Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.
The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.
He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.

title_en: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
title_zh: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
summary: US media reports there are calls to replace Pete Hegseth, who also faces a possible impeachment vote, while Marco Rubio is rumoured to be eyeing a presidential run.
summary_zh: US media reports there are calls to replace Pete Hegseth, who also faces a possible impeachment vote, while Marco Rubio is rumoured to be eyeing a presidential run.
body_en: The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration.
US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses.

One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort.
"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."
Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview.
"I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"
The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news".
The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him.

Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump might be, however, considering ousting General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Centcom chief Admiral Brad Cooper. Both played significant roles in offering guidance on the war, which started eight months ago.
Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.
He told news site Politico that he will trigger his resolution to impeach the defence secretary early next week.

title_en: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
title_zh: 肺癌手术几周后，教皇开始了漫长的拉丁美洲之行
summary: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
summary_zh: 上个月切除了部分肺部的教皇利奥将访问乌拉圭、阿根廷和秘鲁。
body_en: Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Rome

Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
body_zh: 南欧和东欧记者，罗马
教皇利奥十四世在肺癌手术后仅三周，就开始了对拉丁美洲的漫长访问，其中包括万众期待的“返乡”秘鲁，他在那里担任了多年的牧师。
梵蒂冈表示，没有针对教皇的健康采取任何特别措施，称他是一名“接受过手术的71岁老人”，而不是患有“永久性健康状况”的人。
利奥本人上个月透露，医生在例行扫描中发现了肿瘤。肿瘤连同他的右肺下叶一起被切除，他的医疗团队随后证实癌症没有扩散。
此次行程将访问乌拉圭、阿根廷和秘鲁，在罗马举行的新闻发布会上，一位女发言人强调，教皇利奥拥有“惊人的耐力”，并对他“亲自确认的行程……没有任何改变”感到“非常热情”。
维拉诺瓦大学的马西莫·法吉奥利教授告诉英国广播公司：“梵蒂冈此次访问传达的信息是，‘那是一个短暂的插曲，现在我们又回到了正轨’。”他指出，教皇手术后返回工作岗位一直很忙碌。
“过去几天我们看到他发表演讲、观众等等。他看起来状态很好。这很重要。”
不过，12 天的旅程对任何人来说都是艰巨的。它包含多个长途和本地航班，覆盖从亚马逊到安第斯山脉的数千英里。
起点将是乌拉圭，该国的天主教徒人数近年来急剧下降，而教皇四十年来首次访问该国。
随后，利奥前往前任教皇方济各的祖国阿根廷。
“这次访问也是对方济各的致敬，他没有以教皇身份来到阿根廷，”位于罗马的阿根廷国家教堂圣玛丽亚阿多洛拉塔教堂的教区费尔南多·拉古纳神父说。
他告诉英国广播公司：“当利奥教皇此次访问的消息被宣布时，我们所有人的心中都充满了喜悦。” “尽管他生病了，但我一直以为他会去。我认为他从来没有想过取消！”
神父正在罗马教堂内安装一个大屏幕，让教区居民可以从远处观看旅途中的所有关键时刻。这座建筑已经贴满了海报，宣布教皇利奥在阿根廷受到欢迎。 “我们在等你！”，其中一人宣称。
教皇旅程的这一阶段——包括与国家元首的会面以及宗教活动——可能是政治上最敏感的。哈维尔·米莱总统曾称教皇方济各是“地球上的邪恶”和“共产主义者”，因为他提倡帮助穷人的社会正义学说。反过来，阿根廷主教们批评了米莱严厉的紧缩措施，大幅削减了社会支出。
但米雷已经欢迎了教皇利奥，她在 X 上的一篇帖子中写道，阿根廷“怀着巨大的喜悦”等待着。预计将有数百万人前来迎接他。
这次旅行的亮点无疑被留到了最后，即教皇利奥抵达秘鲁——梵蒂冈称其为回归根源。
“他熟悉这些街道，”一位发言人说道。
出生于美国的罗伯特·普雷沃斯特断断续续地在秘鲁度过了近20年，甚至拥有秘鲁公民身份。那段时间被视为塑造他的教皇职位的基础。
他的日程安排包括返回奇克拉约教区，并于 2014 年被任命为主教，直到近十年后方济各将他调往梵蒂冈。
他还将前往印加帝国前首都库斯科，在海拔3000m以上的地方做弥撒，然后前往亚马逊地区的普卡尔帕。

title_en: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
title_zh: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
summary: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.
summary_zh: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.
body_en: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.
Somalia's president: They tried to kill me five times
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.

The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.

title_en: Americans voted against Trump's Iran war. Gulf countries hope that means an end to the conflict
title_zh: 美国人投票反对特朗普的伊朗战争。海湾国家希望这意味着冲突的结束
summary: The US midterm results showed how unpopular Donald Trump's Iran war is. Now, Gulf countries, trapped for months in the middle of the war between the US and Iran, see reason for optimism.
summary_zh: 美国中期选举结果显示，唐纳德·特朗普的伊朗战争是多么不受欢迎。现在，海湾国家被困在美国之间的战争中数月之久。
body_en: After his party's resounding defeat in the US midterm elections this week, President Donald Trump conceded that the war with Iran had likely played a part.

"I think a part of it was Iran, but, at the same time, people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, conceding that US voters were unwilling to accept the impact of the war on gas prices.
Observers say the United States and Israel had been holding off on major attacks on Iran until after both had held elections .
At the end of October, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was already warning Gulf state governments to brace for a short, intense military campaign after the midterms.

While foreign policy is a US president's purview, analysts have pointed out that a Congress controlled by the Democratic party could ostensibly withhold funding for Trump's military expeditions. However newly-elected Democratic politicians won't take their seats until early next year.

As two US professors of political science wrote for Foreign Affairs magazine this week, past American presidents, like Trump, who become "lame ducks" — that is, a president who loses control of Congress and can't run for another term — have often ramped up international interventions.

"As they think about their legacy, lame ducks often turn to foreign policy, where the power of the presidency allows them to act unfettered by pesky domestic politics," they explained. And one of the places where Trump is most likely to act is Iran , the professors argued.
On the other hand, Trump also told several media outlets that he was in "no rush" to start bombing Iran again .
Opinions on Iran's next moves are also divided.

The Iranians have said they're ready for any attack and rhetoric from senior leaders indicates they may be willing to strike a wider range of targets than previously. That could include regional energy and economic infrastructure and even undersea telecommunications cabling or data centers.

If Iran thinks there is an existential threat to its leadership, then "all bets are off," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, or MEI, and an expert on Iran, said during a virtual briefing hosted by MEI this week. "I think they will target differently in the Gulf states [this time] … so it really depends on how all this unfolds."
But other experts believe Iran was deliberately holding out to pressure Trump before the midterms. Now the election is over , the Iranians may be more willing to negotiate a peace deal.
All this leaves the Gulf states, who have been the main targets of Iranian attacks since the conflict began, in a difficult position.

"We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert," Anwar Gargash, a foreign policy adviser to United Arab Emirates leadership, said at a security conference in Bahrain last weekend, the Manama Dialogue hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS. "We are clearly seeking a political off-ramp."

Qatar has been trying to negotiate between the US and Iran but has also been conducting emergency drills at its airport. The Emiratis have been doing similar drills. And Saudi Arabia is looking at a war on two fronts: The oil-rich state is already under attack from the Houthi militia in neighboring Yemen . Even Egypt has reacted, reportedly strengthening air defenses around the Suez Canal.
Still, no matter what happens next, the US-Israel-Iran war has already made Gulf states evaluate defense partnerships with the US. Rather than making them safe, US bases have made them a target.

"There is widespread disappointment across the region with the US over the folly of the war, the erratic nature of Washington's military and diplomatic conduct, and its decision to prioritize Israel's defense over that of its Gulf partners," Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow at the IISS, told news agency Bloomberg this week. "If the US liberation of Kuwait in 1991 was the moment that established America's role in the region, the 2026 war may be remembered as the moment that undid it."
Gulf states are widening their outreach with, for example, the UAE getting closer to Israel and the Saudis entering the Mecca defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.

"The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance," Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London, wrote for online outlet Middle East Eye this week. "A lame-duck Trump will speed that process."
That's even though a Democrat-led Congress might make the US a slightly more reliable partner again.
body_zh: 唐纳德·特朗普总统在其政党本周在美国中期选举中惨败后承认，与伊朗的战争可能是其中的一个原因。
特朗普对福克斯新闻表示：“我认为其中一部分原因是伊朗，但与此同时，人们理解我对伊朗所做的事情的重要性。”他承认美国选民不愿意接受战争对天然气价格的影响。
观察人士称，美国和以色列一直推迟对伊朗发动重大袭击，直到两国都举行了选举。
10月底，《华尔街日报》报道称，特朗普政府已警告海湾国家政府做好中期选举后短暂而激烈的军事行动的准备。
虽然外交政策是美国总统的职权范围，但分析人士指出，民主党控制的国会表面上可能会扣留特朗普军事远征的资金。然而，新当选的民主党政客要到明年初才会就任。
正如两位美国政治学教授本周在《外交事务》杂志上撰文，过去的美国总统，比如特朗普，成为“跛脚鸭”——即失去国会控制权、无法连任的总统——往往会加大国际干预力度。
他们解释说：“当他们思考自己的遗产时，跛脚鸭经常转向外交政策，总统职位的权力使他们能够不受讨厌的国内政治的束缚。”教授们认为，特朗普最有可能采取行动的地方之一是伊朗。
另一方面，特朗普还对多家媒体表示，他“并不急于”再次开始轰炸伊朗。
对于伊朗下一步行动的看法也存在分歧。
伊朗人表示，他们已做好应对任何袭击的准备，高级领导人的言论表明，他们可能愿意打击比以前更广泛的目标。这可能包括区域能源和经济基础设施，甚至海底电信电缆或数据中心。
总部位于华盛顿的中东研究所 (MEI) 高级研究员、伊朗问题专家罗斯·哈里森 (Ross Harrison) 在本周由 MEI 主办的虚拟简报会上表示，如果伊朗认为其领导层面临生存威胁，那么“所有赌注都将落空”。 “我认为（这次）他们在海湾国家的目标会有所不同……所以这实际上取决于这一切如何展开。”
但其他专家认为，伊朗故意在中期选举前向特朗普施压。现在选举已经结束，伊朗人可能更愿意谈判达成和平协议。
所有这些都让海湾国家陷入了困境，这些国家自冲突开始以来一直是伊朗袭击的主要目标。
阿拉伯联合酋长国领导人的外交政策顾问安瓦尔·加尔加什上周末在巴林举行的由国际战略研究所（IISS）主办的麦纳麦对话安全会议上表示：“我们发现自己陷入了一场危机，我们在外交上非常努力地试图避免这场危机。” “我们显然正在寻求政治出口。”
卡塔尔一直试图在美国和伊朗之间进行谈判，但也一直在其机场进行紧急演习。阿联酋人一直在进行类似的演习。沙特阿拉伯正在考虑在两条战线上爆发战争：这个石油资源丰富的国家已经受到邻国也门胡塞民兵的攻击。甚至埃及也做出了反应，据报道加强了苏伊士运河周围的防空。
尽管如此，无论接下来发生什么，美以伊战争已经让海湾国家评估与美国的防务伙伴关系。美国基地非但没有保证他们的安全，反而让他们成为攻击目标。
国际战略研究所高级研究员哈桑·阿尔哈桑本周对彭博社表示：“整个地区对美国普遍感到失望，因为这场战争是愚蠢的，华盛顿的军事和外交行为反复无常，而且美国决定优先考虑以色列的防务而不是海湾伙伴的防务。” “如果说 1991 年美国解放科威特是确立美国在该地区角色的时刻，那么 2026 年的战争可能会被人们铭记为摧毁美国角色的时刻。”
海湾国家正在扩大其影响力，例如，阿联酋与以色列走得更近，沙特与巴基斯坦和土耳其签署了麦加防御协议。
“海湾国家已经走向战略自治和自力更生，”伦敦国王学院安全研究学院高级讲师安德烈亚斯·克里格本周在在线媒体《中东之眼》上写道。 “跛脚鸭特朗普将加速这一进程。”
尽管民主党领导的国会可能会让美国再次成为稍微更可靠的合作伙伴。

title_en: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
title_zh: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
summary_zh: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
body_en: Major construction near Iran bases, satellite images suggest - BBC News
By Shayan Sardarizadeh , Benedict Garman and Matt Murphy , BBC Verify

Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst noted that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

At Karaj and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.

The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", says Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.

The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Sean O'Connor, an analyst with the intelligence firm Janes. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".

The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".

A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.

But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas.

A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.

Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."

Beirut, Lebanon – During Israel’s intensification of its war on Lebanon in March, Aya stayed at her home in Abbasiyeh, in southern Lebanon, despite the risks. At one point, she says, her neighbour’s house was targeted by an Israeli attack.
The attacks have subsided after an ostensible ceasefire was initially announced in April. But the sounds of war have not ceased.

“There’s always drones around and sounds of detonations, but we’ve grown thick skin,” she told Al Jazeera.

In recent weeks, however, fears have intensified around a potential third Israeli intensification since 2024. Many Lebanese are now living in limbo, especially those in areas that previously witnessed intense Israeli attacks.

Aya said her family has prepared extra medication for her grandparents, in case a new round of conflict makes it difficult to obtain. Others are preparing bags and extra food, and keeping their electronic devices charged should the attacks start again.
She also said she would leave her home if Israeli attacks intensified again, rather than stay as she had before.
“I don’t have the energy for this anymore,” she said. Instead, she has been thinking about leaving Lebanon.

“I just can’t handle going through another displacement, especially while watching people around me carry on with their lives as if nothing is happening,” she said. “I know it’s normal, but for me it’s mentally exhausting.”

The Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah and Israel have been at war since October 2023. Since then, Israel has killed around 9,000 people in Lebanon, according to the Lebanese health ministry, mostly during escalations in the autumn of 2024 and in March and April 2026. Israel invaded Lebanon during each offensive and has since occupied up to 10 kilometres of territory , where it has established a so-called “Yellow Line”. Below that line, Israel continues to destroy towns and villages, while it has already made border areas uninhabitable, possibly for years to come .

A ceasefire was announced in April, just over a week after Israel launched more than 100 attacks on Lebanon in less than 10 minutes , killing more than 350 people. Then in June, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement to set up “pilot zones”, as part of which the Israeli military would withdraw from those areas and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah.

Following the ceasefire and framework agreement, active fighting between Hezbollah and Israel has eased, despite Israel’s ongoing attacks and destruction of homes and infrastructure in the far south of Lebanon. Those who live above the Yellow Line are mostly out of the line of fire but hear constant explosions and drones, and at times have struggled to access their land .

In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has reportedly considered launching another round of attacks on Iran, in coordination with Israel. Iran has warned that if such an attack happens, it would retaliate against targets in the region. This has led to questions over whether Hezbollah, which is backed by Iran, would return to conducting its own attacks against Israel.

Israeli officials have also accused the Lebanese army of failing to meet its part of the framework deal – something the Lebanese army denies – in what analysts say might be an effort to build justification for another bombing campaign in Lebanon.

“When it comes to Lebanon, Israel doesn’t need that instigation,” Mohamad Bazzi, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “It destroyed more of the south under the ceasefire of April 17 than before it. Again and again, Israel has shown its willingness to carry out its policies, to destroy as much of south Lebanon as possible, to make it uninhabitable, and to punish the Shia community and there is no reason it won’t do more of the same if the US and Israel restart the Iran war on a large scale.”

In July 2024, Ramez, who did not want to use his real name for security reasons, was sitting in his bedroom in Beirut’s southern suburb of Haret Hreik when he heard loud explosions. Soon after, the neighbouring building collapsed on his apartment .
Since then, he has stayed in his family’s second home, about a half-hour drive southeast of Beirut.

“The war for me never really stopped,” he told Al Jazeera. “Going to sleep is a gamble between insomnia, nightmares or panic attacks. Even if every country in the world disposed of every single bomb and every single bullet and every single gun, the trauma will stay there.”

title_en: How Israel is tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
title_zh: How Israel is tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
summary: Israeli restrictions on teachers and pressure to adopt Israeli curriculum threaten Palestinian education in the city.
summary_zh: Israeli restrictions on teachers and pressure to adopt Israeli curriculum threaten Palestinian education in the city.

Jamal Shalabi is a 66-year-old chemistry teacher living in el-Bireh, in the occupied West Bank, but since 1998 he has taught in occupied East Jerusalem, making the commute through Israeli checkpoints every day.

The process was tiring, but it allowed him to work. But he now fears that soon won’t be the case, after he was informed by his school’s administration that he was one of 180 Palestinian teachers whose travel permits allowing them entry into East Jerusalem would be revoked upon their expiry at the end of the 2026-27 academic year.

The denial of entry permits to teachers is one of the most prominent restrictions imposed by Israel on schools in East Jerusalem, which, like the West Bank, is illegally occupied Palestinian territory, but which Israel considers part of a unified Jerusalem under its control.

Permits were already a problem for teachers like Shalabi this year, when the issuance of documents was delayed until September 15, two weeks after the academic year began. Permits were also delayed last January. The delays in both January and September led to school strikes in East Jerusalem, a move intended to exert pressure and demonstrate a unified stance against these Israeli measures.

Shalabi explained that even when the permits are approved, they are severely restrictive. The documents can only be used during specific hours, which teachers are not permitted to exceed. The teachers are also prohibited from being anywhere other than the schools.

“These permit restrictions have been in place since the war on Gaza in 2023; we can no longer reach the Al-Aqsa Mosque to pray, nor can we accompany students on school field trips, as the permits are strictly limited to the workplace,” he explained.
“Moreover, for the first time, we were barred from entering Jerusalem for an entire week during the recent Jewish holiday of Sukkot,” he added.

The permit restrictions come alongside wider measures affecting Palestinian education in East Jerusalem, including policies introduced under a plan approved by the Israeli government supposedly aimed at “reducing socioeconomic gaps” in East Jerusalem, whose population is majority Palestinian, despite Israeli efforts to increase the number of Jewish settlers.

The government plan also aims to increase the number of Palestinian students studying the Israeli curriculum. It does so by conditioning funding for new schools on the adoption of the Israeli curriculum, alongside programmes to train teachers within the Israeli education system.

A report by the Israeli human rights organisation Ir Amim warned that the policies exploit educational needs to undermine the autonomy of Palestinian education, as well as its national and cultural identity.

The report further warns of the repercussions of a law that prohibits the employment of teachers who hold university degrees from Palestinian educational institutions, a measure likely to exacerbate the existing shortage of teachers in East Jerusalem’s schools.
According to Ir Amim, approximately half of the education budget allocated under the Israeli government’s plan for East Jerusalem is directed towards expanding the teaching of the Israeli curriculum.

Furthermore, Israeli authorities make the adoption of this curriculum a prerequisite for the opening of new state-funded schools, which the organisation views as a form of pressure on both schools and parents to abandon the Palestinian curriculum.
The number of Palestinian students in East Jerusalem studying the Israeli curriculum was only in the hundreds 15 years ago. But by 2020, the figure had risen to more than 10,000.

The numbers have risen sharply since then. By 2024, it had risen to almost 20,000, according to Palestinian officials, and then to more than 27,000 the following year, according to figures cited by Ir Amim. Palestinian officials estimate that more than 45,000 students – approximately 38 percent of the total student population in the city – are now studying the Israeli curriculum in the 2026-27 academic year.

A principal of a school in East Jerusalem, who requested anonymity for fear of repercussions from Israeli authorities, told Al Jazeera that the expansion of the Israeli curriculum to tens of thousands of Palestinian students is the culmination of years of policies aimed at controlling education in East Jerusalem.

title_en: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
title_zh: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".
summary_zh: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".
body_en: By Kelly Ng and Abel U , BBC Chinese , Reporting from Macau
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".

Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.

Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.

Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

Kozo Tashima first started playing football after watching the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and since then he has dedicated his life to developing the sport’s growth in Japan.
The 68-year-old is set to become the first person from Japan to run for the FIFA presidency after announcing he would stand against Gianni Infantino in football’s governing body’s election in March.

Tashima has served as a football player, coach and bureaucrat and has a reputation for being a safe pair of hands.
He rarely makes headlines, and one of the few times he appeared outside the sport pages was when he became one of the first public figures in Japan to contract coronavirus in March 2020.
He spent time studying at the German Sport University Cologne and said the experience changed the way he saw sport’s purpose in society.
He says his decision to run for the FIFA presidency was based on a belief that “in this age of business and money, sport must firmly uphold its integrity”.
“The worst thing would be if he [Infantino] were to continue without an election,” he told reporters after announcing his candidacy.
“I feel this is a test of whether FIFA has the ability to cleanse itself.”
Tashima was born in southern Kumamoto and captained his team to the title in Japan’s prestigious national high school championship.
With no professional football in the country at the time, he had ambitions of becoming a PE teacher and enrolled at a university, where he was called up to play for Japan’s full national team.
He joined a club in Japan’s amateur league after graduating but soon retired as a player and went to Germany to study to become a coach.
He described his “profound shock” at the players’ superior skills and the way football was viewed there.
“Even back in 1980, the training in Germany was hugely scientific and systematic,” he said.
“Everything seemed like a different world from Japan, and it was a big culture shock for me.”
Tashima returned home determined to use what he had learned in Germany and help develop Japanese football.
He coached a university team before joining the Japan Football Association (JFA), where he worked on development programmes and coached the country’s national teams at various youth levels.

Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.

In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.

Thousands of Paraguayans gathered outside Congress on Thursday to protest against Peña. Lawmakers voted unanimously on Thursday to launch impeachment proceedings against Peña over the crisis, alleging misconduct and a conflict of interest in dealings with the bank to which he is tied.

Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.

The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.

The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.

Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.
Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.

“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.
Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.
“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.

“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.
Since the scandal broke, Peña has insisted in interviews and statements that he committed no wrongdoing.
body_zh: 圣地亚哥·佩纳的右翼政府授权上野银行在倒闭前大幅扩大业务
巴拉圭右翼总统圣地亚哥·佩纳周四辞职，此前几天政治和金融危机导致南美国家银行系统崩溃。
危机的中心是上野银行，在佩纳领导下的短短几年内，该银行从一家默默无闻的数字银行发展成为该国最大的银行之一，声称拥有巴拉圭约 60% 的成年人口作为客户。
上周一，央行命令上野就破产问题进行解决，冻结了 300 万客户的存款，导致数十万家庭无法获得食物和基本日常开支。银行高管被捕，人们走上街头进行大规模抗议。
林奇夫人：一位爱尔兰女性如何加入巴拉圭英雄行列
这位 47 岁的经济学家自 2023 年 8 月开始执政，任期至 2028 年，但他已经面临得到广泛支持的弹劾程序。
佩尼亚在视频中表示：“亲爱的同胞们，今天，我在我一生中最困难的时刻之一向你们发表讲话。我的心全在巴拉圭，并坚信我们的共和国必须始终优先于任何人或情况，因此我决定辞去共和国总统职务。”
上野银行 (Ueno Bank) 最初是一家金融公司，成立于 2021 年，并于 2021 年被巴拉圭最大的商业和工业集团之一 Grupo Vázquez 收购。 2023 年底，它获得了佩尼亚管理下的中央银行的授权，可以作为数字银行运营。
该银行迅速扩大业务，通过慷慨的杂货现金返还优惠吸引客户，并赞助巴拉圭国家足球队。周三，球员们发表了一封信，“要求”政府和司法系统做出“强有力的回应”。
该银行开始管理来自国家和养老金实体（包括退休基金）的 8 亿至 8.5 亿美元存款，由于佩纳之前与上野控股的持股关系，引发了有关利益冲突的批评。
佩纳表示，作为一名经济学家，他只是进行了一次“投资”，但他已经出售了所有股份。当当地媒体指出国家和养老基金向该银行提供可能存在不当偏袒时，他称这是一场旨在削弱政府的“虚假媒体运动”。
周三，反对派议员甚至佩纳所在的科罗拉多党成员提出弹劾动议，要求总统对此次垮台负责。直到去年初，他一直是该银行运营集团的股东，据报道，最近几个月，他一直无视央行和媒体对其运营的警告。
周四上午，当他的前盟友、前总统奥拉西奥·卡特斯发布支持弹劾的消息时，政治压力加剧。
“我们不会站在盗窃公共、私人和养老金领取者资金的一边。我们必须考虑到人民以及我们在科罗拉多党中所坚持的价值观。我们支持弹劾共和国总统圣地亚哥·佩纳，以恢复共和国的制度秩序，”他写道。
当佩纳发布宣布辞职的视频后，其他议员也纷纷效仿，开始讨论弹劾问题。
这位现任前总统说：“我这样做是考虑到我们国家的稳定、社会和平以及维护我们民主制度的必要性。”
“如果我在任何时候让人民失望，我也想向他们道歉……但今天我的首要任务只有一件事：让巴拉圭人安心，他们将自己的储蓄托付给我们的金融体系……我最大的愿望是保证这些资金的归还，”他补充道。
自丑闻爆发以来，佩纳在采访和声明中坚称自己没有任何不当行为。

title_en: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
title_zh: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
summary_zh: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
body_en: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
It is unclear whether this action could be reversed by a future president or a legal challenge.
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.

The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".

"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said, adding that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.
Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone.
Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.
Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".
How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image
The entire building is already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.
The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.
The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.
As president, Trump has the power to create national monuments, which are similar to national parks.
Trump's order calls on the office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".

It notes the existing protections to the White House, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".

Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".
"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he told the BBC.

title_en: How elderly ‘unsung heroes’ powered Lula’s historic fightback in Brazil
title_zh: 年长的“无名英雄”如何为卢拉在巴西的历史性反击提供动力
summary: Older voters praised for helping tip balance in leftwing president’s favour against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her ho
summary_zh: 年长选民因在决选中帮助左翼总统对极右翼弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗的支持而受到赞扬，这已经过去了近十年的时间。
body_en: Older voters praised for helping tip balance in leftwing president’s favour against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff
It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.

But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
Soares clung to the banister as, step by step, she climbed two flights of stairs to the polling booth under the watchful eye of her granddaughter’s husband, Marcio Marques.
Inside, the frail but jaunty centenarian keyed the number “13” – representing Bolsonaro’s leftwing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – into an electronic voting machine and pressed confirm.
“I like Lula. I really do!” enthused Soares, a retired bank employee who has lived in Rio de Janeiro most of her life.

“I don’t like Bolsonaro or his father. So the efficient thing to do was go out and vote,” Soares added, as her grandsons, Tito and Ravi, played on the balcony around her surrounded by pot plants and books.
Soares is one of more than 1 million elderly people who, having missed the election’s 4 October first round – which Lula lost – decided to vote in the second.

Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round loser bounced back, but Lula did just that. And after Lula’s shock revival, elderly voters have been hailed as the election’s unsung heroes – including by Lula himself.

At his 81st birthday party last week, the leftist veteran shed tears while describing his gratitude to the elderly people who helped him clinch a historic fourth term while clutching walking frames and sticks.

“I honestly think it was the most powerful and human image I’ve ever seen during an election,” Lula said of viral pictures showing voters in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried into polling centres by relatives or carers, some in stretchers or wheelchairs.

In north-east Brazil, where Lula was born into rural poverty in the 1940s, a 114-year-old retiree called Josefa Pereira da Conceição went to vote wearing a red T-shirt emblazoned with Lula’s face and the slogan “Strength of the people”.
Election experts are still crunching the numbers to fully understand how Lula pulled off his unprecedented fightback, finding 10.3m extra votes between the first and second rounds.

Explanations include a sharp increase in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote; an extraordinary digital mobilisation involving a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11m members in less than a month; and a student-led street rebellion in which millions of citizens protested across Brazil.

Some believe elderly people were also crucial, noting how 1.4 million of the 3 million extra voters who took part in the second round after skipping the first were over 70. Pre-election polls suggested such voters were more inclined to vote for Lula.

Speaking at Lula’s victory celebration, the former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph which sent a message to the democratic world. “It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” Tebet declared, claiming: “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”

The political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said there was concrete evidence of higher turnout among older voters in the runoff, particularly those aged 60 to 79. Voting is only mandatory in Brazil for those aged 18 to 69.

“The images [of elderly people voting] aren’t misleading: they reveal a phenomenon that isn’t just an isolated case. It’s not some made-up story or a staged example. It really happened – and it was a movement you can measure statistically,” Toledo said of the images suggesting an unusually large number of older voters.

That said, Toledo believed the swing to Lula was explained mostly by fear, not age. Voting data suggested many people who backed Lula in the runoff had previously voted for Bolsonaro’s rightwing adversaries, hoping to protest against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), which has governed for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.
body_zh: 年长选民因在决选中帮助左翼总统对极右翼弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗的支持而受到赞扬
距离西莉亚·德奥利维拉·苏亚雷斯上次投票已经过去了近十年，距离这位 101 岁高龄的曾祖母上次离开家也有几个月了。
但10月25日，当巴西举行了许多人认为是几十年来最重要的总统选举时，苏亚雷斯的亲戚帮助她坐上轮椅，并开车送她到附近的一所学校，以确保极右翼候选人弗拉维奥·博索纳罗(Flávio Bolsonaro)不会获胜。
苏亚雷斯紧紧抓住栏杆，在孙女丈夫马西奥·马克斯的注视下，一步步爬上两层楼梯来到投票站。
在里面，这位虚弱但乐观的百岁老人在电子投票机中输入数字“13”——代表博尔索纳罗的左翼竞争对手、总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦——并按下确认键。
“我喜欢卢拉。我真的很喜欢！”苏亚雷斯是一位退休银行员工，她大半生都住在里约热内卢，她对此非常兴奋。
“我不喜欢博尔索纳罗或他的父亲。所以最有效的做法就是出去投票，”苏亚雷斯补充道，她的孙子蒂托和拉维在她周围的阳台上玩耍，周围环绕着盆栽植物和书籍。
苏亚雷斯是超过 100 万老年人之一，他们错过了 10 月 4 日的第一轮选举（卢拉输掉了选举），但决定在第二轮投票。
自 20 世纪 80 年代民主回归以来，第一轮失败者从未出现过反弹，但卢拉做到了。在卢拉令人震惊的复兴之后，老年选民被誉为选举中的无名英雄——包括卢拉本人。
上周，在他的 81 岁生日聚会上，这位左翼退伍军人攥着助行架和手杖，流下了眼泪，向帮助他赢得历史性第四个任期的老年人表示感谢。
“老实说，我认为这是我在选举期间见过的最有力、最人性化的形象，”卢拉在谈到病毒照片时说道，这些照片显示 80 多岁、90 多岁和 100 多岁的选民被亲戚或护理人员抬进投票中心，其中一些人坐在担架或轮椅上。
20 世纪 40 年代，卢拉出生在巴西东北部的贫困农村，一位名叫 Josefa Pereira da Conceição 的 114 岁退休老人穿着印有卢拉头像和“人民的力量”口号的红色 T 恤去投票。
选举专家仍在处理数据，以充分了解卢拉如何实现前所未有的反击，发现第一轮和第二轮之间额外增加了 1030 万张选票。
解释包括投票前夕福利金大幅增加；一场非同寻常的数字动员，涉及支持卢拉的 WhatsApp 群组，该群组在不到一个月的时间里成员数量从 5 万名增加到近 1100 万；学生领导的街头叛乱，巴西各地数百万公民举行抗议活动。
一些人认为老年人也很重要，他们指出，在跳过第一轮后参加第二轮的 300 万额外选民中，有 140 万年龄超过 70 岁。选前民意调查显示，这些选民更倾向于投票给卢拉。
前部长西蒙娜·特贝特在卢拉的胜利庆典上发表讲话，称这一结果是跨代人的胜利，向民主世界传递了一个信息。特贝特宣称：“抵抗法西斯主义是可能的——你所需要做的就是动员社会，年轻人走上街头，黄金老人拯救了我们的民主。”
政治记者何塞·罗伯托·德托莱多表示，有具体证据表明，决选中老年选民的投票率较高，尤其是 60 至 79 岁的选民。在巴西，只有 18 至 69 岁的选民必须投票。
“[老年人投票]的图像并不具有误导性：它们揭示的现象不仅仅是一个孤立的案例。这不是一些编造的故事或一个上演的例子。它确实发生过——而且这是一场你可以用统计数据衡量的运动，”托莱多在谈到这些图像时说，这些图像表明老年选民的数量异常多。
尽管如此，托莱多认为转向卢拉的主要原因是恐惧，而不是年龄。投票数据显示，许多在决选中支持卢拉的人此前曾投票给博尔索纳罗的右翼对手，希望抗议卢拉领导的工人党(PT)，该党在过去24年中执政近18年。

title_zh: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
summary: Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said. The spiders were hidden inside dirty
summary_zh: Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said. The spiders were hidden inside dirty
body_en: Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.

The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.

They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

title_en: Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
title_zh: 土耳其西部连环枪击事件造成八人死亡
summary: Victims are found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
summary_zh: 据当地报道，在多个地点发现了三辆不同车辆中的受害者。
body_en: Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in Eskişehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.

Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.

In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".
body_zh: 土耳其西部发生一系列枪击事件，造成八人死亡、一人重伤。
据当地报道，袭击于周四在阿菲永卡拉希萨尔省发生，在多个地点发现了三辆不同车辆中的受害者。
嫌疑人逃跑，引发追捕，当局后来表示他已在埃斯基谢希尔省被捕。
土耳其媒体发布的闭路电视录像显示，一名身穿黑色夹克、白色裤子、戴着眼镜的男子站在一辆红色小型货车旁，手里拿着一把长武器。
土耳其国营阿纳多卢通讯社报道称，阿亚齐尼村附近有三人被杀，基耶尔村附近还有三人被杀。在尤卡里坦迪尔，两名妇女被发现受伤，后来在医院死亡。
当地媒体称，通往受影响村庄的道路已被警方封闭，同时警方展开大规模行动寻找嫌疑人。
据《国民报》报道，据称袭击者劫持的一辆汽车后来被发现陷在泥里——嫌疑人在步行逃离之前将其遗弃。
阿菲永卡拉希萨尔省在社交媒体上发布的一份声明中表示，“我们州所有相关机构从一开始就一直在协调工作，并正在认真开展必要的工作”。

title_en: Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win
title_zh: Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win
summary: His historic victory in Michigan shows that Muslim Americans need not abandon their identity to succeed in politics.
summary_zh: His historic victory in Michigan shows that Muslim Americans need not abandon their identity to succeed in politics.
body_en: Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win | US Midterm Elections 2026 | Al Jazeera
Share Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to win on social media

Messages popped up on my WhatsApp account from New York, Gaza, Pakistan and Australia. Friends and colleagues were following Michigan’s Senate race, talking excitedly about Abdul El-Sayed. As the results from Wayne County sealed his victory on Tuesday, I felt something I had rarely felt before in American politics: not a muted relief that someone had lost but genuine joy and hope that someone had won.

El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, defeated Republican Mike Rogers . He will be the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate. As a Muslim American from Michigan, this hit home.

Like many in Michigan’s Muslim community, I knew of Abdul long before he became a fixture in national headlines, from his 2018 gubernatorial campaign to his Friday sermons in local mosques. As Ramadan began this year, I attended one of his town halls for Muslim constituents. Before a few dozen community members and leaders, Abdul pledged to fight for all Michiganders. His sincerity and commitment to that pledge remained evident even as the pressures of the campaign intensified. I have seen him attend funerals for community members near my home and watched him go from person to person, greeting people with kindness. Even in the final days of an exhausting campaign, he responded personally to messages from the community, including mine.

We attended the same university, the University of Michigan, where he once helped lead the Muslim Students’ Association. I later served as a college student body president there. Just days before the election, Muslim alumni (including me) invited him to a football tailgate party with students, parents and graduates. His former teachers and students have spoken to me with pride about the person they knew.

Muslim Americans are often asked to celebrate any politician who occasionally says “salaam” or appears in a mosque before Election Day. Abdul was not an outsider to our community coming to court us. He belonged to it.

During the campaign, I welcomed hundreds of local Muslim community members, out-of-state political candidates canvassing for him and members of his staff into my home. People heard from those closest to him what this race could mean for Muslim Americans. The enthusiasm felt different from the familiar, dispiriting bargain of voting mainly to stop someone worse.

Two years ago, I wrote about why I would vote against genocide in the 2024 presidential election. That decision was shaped by my work with Palestinian healthcare workers, by witnessing the realities in Palestine firsthand and by outrage at the Biden-Harris administration’s complicity in the genocide in Gaza. Neither I nor many of Michigan’s Muslims have forgotten. But this time, the ballot offered something other than just a protest vote: a candidate who had opposed Israel’s genocide against Palestinians from the outset while also caring about the range of issues affecting Michiganders.

His willingness to speak truth to power attracted immense hostility from Washington’s elites. President Donald Trump repeatedly mocked Abdul’s name , treating “Muhammad” – his middle name, meaning “the praised one” – as an insult. Political opponents and even some voters insinuated that his faith alone made him suspect, recycling unsubstantiated allegations tying him to groups and movements he did not belong to.

Abdul responded with dignity and directness. When critics made his name the issue, he spoke about groceries, housing, healthcare and affordability. When challenged over his opposition to genocide, he questioned the premise that wanting children to live free of bombs was somehow hateful. He did not accept the proposition that a Muslim must disown his community or Palestine to qualify for public office.

And most importantly, he fought back. Many Muslim voters I spoke to felt they had found someone willing to fight for them, to challenge the presumptions and racism of journalists, pundits and media outlets rather than accept their unjust framing.

His victory speech began with the words his opponents had tried to weaponise: “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.” He recalled having said “inshallah” – “God willing” – whenever he was asked about winning. Now, he said, it was time for “alhamdulillah”, or “Praise be to God.”

That moment was electric, not because Arabic phrases alone are a sign of solidarity – even former President Joe Biden said “inshallah” in a debate before proceeding to commit genocide against Palestinians and aid the bombing of mosques and burning of Qurans – but because his Muslim identity had survived a countrywide effort by special interest groups and racists to make it disqualifying. His faith, Islam, is a value system he actively chooses every day, a commitment he strives to live out in public life. His being Muslim mattered to me more than his Arab ethnicity or ancestral origins, a simple happenstance of birth.

There was money behind the attempt to stop him too. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s (AIPAC’s) affiliated super PAC spent roughly $30m in Michigan’s Democratic primary, an extraordinary investment to defeat someone who openly opposed US support for Israel’s genocide and apartheid. In his victory speech, Abdul thanked AIPAC for the chance to beat it twice. One loss will not dissolve the lobbying group’s power. But Michigan demonstrated that AIPAC spending need not amount to a veto over who can win.

After Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York , sceptics suggested that a Muslim candidate outspoken about Palestine could only win in a liberal metropolis, not a state that Trump carried in 2024. El-Sayed travelled from small towns and villages to industrial cities and suburbs, visiting churches and mosques, and he won statewide.

Michigan has long been a centre of Muslim American life, from Dearborn’s famous Arab restaurants and coffee houses to Hamtramck, the first Muslim-majority city in the US. Generations have built mosques, schools, businesses and institutions while enduring suspicion and discrimination. There is irony in Michigan electing a Muslim alumnus of the University of Michigan, which has faced legal challenges over its treatment of antigenocide protesters. Some of the voices that were treated as dangerous on campus found a home at the ballot box for the first time.

Other Muslims across the country made history too. My mentor, friend and colleague Adam Hamawy, with whom I served on a medical mission in Palestine documenting harm to people’s health, won his congressional race in New Jersey and travelled to Michigan to support Abdul. Darializa Avila Chevalier, Aber Kawas, Nabeela Syed and so many others won seats in Congress and state legislatures across the country, refusing to accept that their silence on human rights abuses is the price of participation.
